body:
If I understand that correctly, you're using a (0, 0)-(640, 360) coordinate system in cavas_items mode at 4x scale, so your actual output is 2560x1440?

If so, then the reason would probably be that a control of height 18.5 in a (640x360) system has a screen height of 74 pixels on a 2560x1440 screen, so it already is on a pixel boundary and snapping doesn't change anything. If you then take a screenshot of that and scale it down by a factor of 4, you end up with a height of 18.5 pixels for that control, which makes it appear blurry in Aseprite.

If you've got a requirement that your output needs to remain crisp after external downscaling by a factor of 4, then you need to make sure that all your screen positions and sizes are evenly divisible by four (at 4x scaling, this would mean they have to be integers in your scene coordinates). In that case, however, you might as well use viewport mode and render at 1/4 scale directly.

Correct about the resolution. The editor shows the heights as 19, while running the game it shows as 18.5, causing the issues. Using viewport stretching is _almost_ perfect, but as mentioned it occasionally results in some pixel rows being lost during rendering, though I think it's possible that that issue only appears after switching from canvas_items stretching to viewport stretching at runtime.

Another side-effect of this issue is that embedded subwindows cause weird issues when using canvas_items stretching on the main viewport:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7a55c0b9-fa1c-4799-ad41-a4db957f2b9d)

EDIT: For clarity, the "Snap Controls to Pixel" correctly snaps to viewport pixel (except in the above SubWindow case), instead of the expected internal pixel coordinate. It does not render on non-integer pixels within the viewport.

EDIT2: I tried wrapping my entire MainMenu scene in a SubViewportContainer with stretch enabled, and a SubViewport child with "Snap Controls to Pixel" and it is very broken. The main viewport is in canvas_items stretch mode. On my 1080p monitor, I get this (with dropdown options being stretched):

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/885deba3-8c8d-4741-8dd4-39aebf87c99a)

And on my 1440p monitor, it looks like this:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/22096028-48f0-42cc-9f8c-9c8fa2fd5103)

And enabling "Snap 2D Vertices to Pixel":

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d6020e93-b9e5-40fb-a6a0-7a0e3dc4a143)

It's not easy to comment on layout and scaling troubles from screenshots alone without knowing how those screenshots were created. Ideally, you could come up with a minimum reproduction project that demonstrates one of your issues. Then we could work out if there's a problem in the engine or if the project needs to be changed to achieve the desired effect.

For a general recommendation: It sounds like you're trying to render your game at 640x360 and then just upscale it to whatever the screen resolution is. If so, use viewport scaling mode (that means selecting "viewport" in the project settings under Display/Window/Stretch/Mode - don't add any SubViewports or SubViewportContainers to the scene itself). If you don't actually use the higher resolution of canvas_items mode for anything, then staying at 640x360 throughout can save you a lot of headache.

Right, switching to viewport stretching mode fixes most issues, but it does prevent me from having subpixel camera movement. I pretty much just wanted UI at 640x360 but using a SubViewport for that causes the issues above. I'll work on an MRP soon.

Yes, smooth camera movement is certainly one reason for wanting a 640x360 game that's secretly a higher resolution. I suppose there is a world where you combine the two by having the game render into a SubViewport at 641x361 (to account for the border pixels needed for smooth scrolling... although odd viewport sizes feel illegal, so maybe make that 642x362) with a camera that uses only integral coordinates (so that in the 642x362 world everything remains on a pixel border) and then have another camera looking at the SubViewport and offset it by the fractional part of the camera position (only moving between (0, 0) and (1, 1)). If you restrict that camera to a number of locations corresponding to the final scaling factor (so on a 1440p display, allow only 0, 0.25, 0.5, and 0.75), you should end up with a view that's both pixel-perfect in the 360p world of the game itself and pixel-perfect in the 1440p world of the screen.

If that sounds too complicated: For my game, I decided to render to 1080p but scale most of the game content by 5x and manually align most things to 5-pixel increments (or rather: to integers in a scaled coordinate system). That way, the game looks a lot like 384x216, but the camera can move smoothly and character sprites can move smoothly and at even diagonal speeds of 1.4 pixels per frame (and are only snapped when they stop walking) and I can overlay higher-resolution 3D objects or the occasional high-res image.
Can you test [4.4.beta1](https://godotengine.org/article/dev-snapshot-godot-4-4-beta-1/)? It includes https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/97745 which 4.4.dev7 didn't.

With 4.4.beta1, the embedded subwindows now render correctly! Perfect timing.
